summary: Psalm 80 is a communal plea for God to restore a devastated people. It begins by asking the Shepherd of Israel to shine out and save, then describes tears, mockery, and anger before turning to a vine image: God once brought the vine from Egypt and planted it, but now its walls are broken and it is ravaged. The repeated cry, “Turn us again,” frames the chapter as a prayer for renewed life and rescue.
whyItMatters: This psalm belongs to Book III of Psalms, the section that often faces sanctuary, national collapse, and the failure of visible security. It gives a community language for asking God to remember what God planted without pretending the ruin is small.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with Asaph; in Psalms, such headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, collection, or performance setting, and their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public and private prayer.
context.date: Psalms is a collection formed over time; individual poems may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period. The precise date of this psalm’s communal distress is uncertain.
context.setting: The poem speaks from communal distress and uses Israel’s memory of being brought from Egypt and planted like a vine in the land.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic lament with refrain, petition, and extended metaphor.

outline.heading: Call to the Shepherd
outline.note: The psalm asks the Shepherd of Israel to hear, shine out, stir up might, and save.

outline.heading: Tears and Contempt
outline.note: The community asks how long God’s anger will continue while the people eat and drink tears and become mocked by enemies.

outline.heading: The Planted Vine
outline.note: The psalm remembers God bringing a vine out of Egypt, planting it, and letting it fill the land.

outline.heading: The Ravaged Vine
outline.note: The vine’s walls are broken, passersby pluck it, and wild creatures ravage it.

outline.heading: Look Down and Visit
outline.note: The prayer asks God to see and tend the vine that God planted, now burned and cut down.

outline.heading: Revive Us Again
outline.note: The psalm asks for God’s hand to be on the strengthened man and closes with a promise to call on God’s name if revived.

keyVerses.text: Turn us again, God. Cause your face to shine, and we will be saved.
keyVerses.why: This is the psalm’s first refrain and states the central request: restoration, God’s favorable presence, and rescue.

keyVerses.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it.
keyVerses.why: This verse begins the vine image and ties the community’s present plea to the memory of God’s earlier rescue and planting.

keyVerses.text: Turn again, we beg you, God of Armies. Look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vine,
keyVerses.why: The verse turns the vine image into direct petition, asking God to attend to what has been damaged.

keyVerses.text: Turn us again, Yahweh God of Armies. Cause your face to shine, and we will be saved.
keyVerses.why: The final refrain repeats the chapter’s plea with its fullest address to God, leaving the reader with the unresolved request for salvation.

themes: A community asking to be restored
Revival and renewed calling on God’s name

questions.question: Who is speaking in Psalm 80?
questions.answer: The psalm speaks as a community, using “us,” “we,” and “your people.” It asks God to save the people, not just one private sufferer. The heading associates the psalm with Asaph, but the body of the poem is communal prayer.

questions.question: Why does the psalm call God “Shepherd of Israel”?
questions.answer: Verse 1 asks the Shepherd of Israel to hear and describes God as leading Joseph like a flock. The image presents God as the one responsible for guiding and caring for the people. The same verse also speaks of God sitting above the cherubim, so the prayer combines shepherd care with royal or sanctuary imagery.

questions.question: What does the repeated line “Turn us again” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The refrain appears in verses 3, 7, and 19 with small changes in the address to God. In this psalm, the phrase is tied to God causing his face to shine and the people being saved. The chapter does not spell out every action involved, but it clearly asks God to restore the community from distress.

questions.question: Why does the psalm say God is angry “against the prayer” of the people?
questions.answer: Verse 4 asks how long God will be angry against the prayer of his people, which makes the suffering sharper: even prayer feels blocked. The psalm does not explain the cause of the anger. It simply voices the community’s experience that distress continues even while they are praying.

questions.question: What is the vine?
questions.answer: The vine is the main image for the people God brought out of Egypt and planted. Verses 8-11 describe the vine growing large enough to fill the land, cover mountains with shadow, and send branches to the sea and the River. The image is poetic, so readers should not press every detail as if it were a map, but the movement is from rescue and planting to growth.

questions.question: What happened to the vine’s walls?
questions.answer: Verse 12 asks why God has broken down the vine’s walls, leaving it exposed to anyone passing by. Verse 13 continues the image with a boar and wild animals feeding on it. The psalm depicts the people as unprotected and ravaged, but it does not name one specific invading power inside the chapter.

questions.question: Who is “the man of your right hand” in verse 17?
questions.answer: Verse 17 asks God’s hand to be on “the man of your right hand” and “the son of man whom you made strong for yourself.” Readers differ on whether this refers to Israel as God’s strengthened people, a king or representative leader, or a figure later readers connect with messianic hope. The chapter itself keeps the wording poetic and does not identify the figure by name.

questions.question: Does the psalm promise that the people will change if God revives them?
questions.answer: Verse 18 says, “So we will not turn away from you,” and asks, “Revive us, and we will call on your name.” The order matters: the community asks God for life and restoration, and then describes renewed faithfulness and prayer. The psalm presents dependence on God’s action rather than confidence in the people’s strength alone.

questions.question: Why does the final refrain use “Yahweh God of Armies”?
questions.answer: The refrain grows in address across the psalm: “God” in verse 3, “God of Armies” in verse 7, and “Yahweh God of Armies” in verse 19. This gives the closing appeal a fuller and more solemn address. The request itself remains the same: God’s shining face and salvation.

glossary.def: A title in verse 1 that pictures God as the one who leads and cares for Israel like a flock.
Heavenly beings named in verse 1, where God is described as sitting above them.
A repeated address to God in this psalm, used in the pleas for restoration and rescue.
The image used for the people God brought out of Egypt, planted, and is asked to visit and restore.
A wild animal in verse 13 that represents the ravaging of the exposed vine.
